text: Ruth Wilson Gilmore, born on April 2, 1950, in New Haven, Connecticut, is a prison abolitionist and prison scholar. She serves as the Director of the Center for Place, Culture, and Politics and is a professor of geography in Earth and Environmental Sciences at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York. Gilmore has made significant contributions to carceral geography, defined as the study of the interrelationships across space, institutions, and political economy that shape and define modern incarceration. She received the 2020 Lifetime Achievement Award from the American Association of Geographers. Born in New Haven, Wilson’s grandfather organized the first blue collar workers' union at Yale University; her father, Courtland Seymour Wilson, was a tool-and-die maker for Winchester Repeating Arms Company and was active in the machinists' union, later serving as assistant dean of student affairs at Yale Medical School and working in the Office of Government and Community Relations at Yale-New Haven Hospital. In 1960, she attended a private school in New Haven as one of its few working-class students and the first, and mostly only, African American student. In 1968, she enrolled at Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania, where she became involved in campus activism; in 1969, she, Fania Davis (the younger sister of radical activist Angela Davis), and other students occupied the school's admissions office to advocate for admitting more Black students. After the sudden death of the university president, white students spread false rumors blaming the occupying students, and the next morning, Gilmore learned that her cousin, John Huggins, and Black Panther Bunchy Carter had been murdered at the University of California, Los Angeles. Following these events, she left Swarthmore and returned home to New Haven, where she enrolled at Yale and earned a bachelor's degree in drama. Gilmore earned her Ph.D. from Rutgers University in 1998 in economic geography and social theory, inspired by Neil Smith. After completing her Ph.D., she was hired as an assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley, where she began developing her concept of carceral geography, which examines the relationships between landscape, natural resources, political economy, infrastructure, and the policing, jailing, caging, and controlling of populations. The academic community in this field is associated with the Carceral Geography Working Group (CGWG) of the Royal Geographical Society with the Institute of British Geographers, and Gilmore delivered a keynote address at the 2nd International Conference for Carceral Geography at the University of Birmingham, UK, on December 12, 2017. She is a cofounder of numerous social justice organizations, including the California Prison Moratorium Project and, in 1998, Critical Resistance alongside Angela Davis. In 2003, she co-founded Californians United for a Responsible Budget (CURB) to oppose jail and prison construction and currently serves on its board. Gilmore is a leading scholar and speaker on prisons, decarceration, racial capitalism, oppositional movements, and state-making. She authored the book Golden Gulag, which won the Lora Romero First Book Publication Prize for the best book in American Studies from the American Studies Association in 2008. Her work has been published in journals such as Race & Class, The Professional Geographer, Social Justice, Global Lockdown: Race, Gender, and the Prison Industrial Complex, and the critical anthology The Revolution Will Not Be Funded: Beyond the Non-Profit Industrial Complex, edited by the Incite! collective. In 2011, she was the keynote speaker at the National Women's Studies Association annual conference in Atlanta, Georgia. In 2012, the American Studies Association awarded her its first Angela Y. Davis Prize for Public Scholarship, recognizing scholars who apply their scholarship to the public good through education, policy influence, or addressing inequalities. In 2014, she received the Harold M. Rose Award for Anti-Racism Research and Practice from the Association of American Geographers. In 2017, she earned the American Studies Association Richard A. Yarborough Award for excellence in teaching and mentoring. In 2020, Prospect listed her as the seventh-greatest thinker for the COVID-19 era, noting that she has spent nearly 30 years developing carceral geography and has helped shift the conversation about crime from punishment to rehabilitation, making her radical ideas especially relevant as the U.S. justice system's failures come to light. An Antipode journal documentary film highlighted her work on geography, racial capitalism, the prison industrial complex, and abolition geographies. In 2021, she was elected a Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 2023, she was honored with a mural painted by artist and filmmaker Jess X. Snow and local community members on the outside of the Possible Futures bookstore in New Haven, Connecticut.
